contentHtml:
KENYA—Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Teaching and Referral Hospital (JOOTRH) has unveiled a KSh30.05 billion (US$231.1 million) master plan to develop a 2,000-bed medical city in Kisumu over ten years, expanding specialised healthcare services and strengthening its regional referral capacity.

The project aims to upgrade the hospital towards Level Six status by expanding inpatient capacity, improving clinical services and modernising supporting infrastructure.

It will be implemented in three phases, with an estimated annual investment requirement of KSh3.01 billion (US$23.15 million).

New medical ward to address congestion

The first phase will include construction of a four-storey, 240-bed medical ward block at an estimated cost of KSh280 million (US$2.15 million).

The project is expected to take two years to complete and will increase inpatient capacity, ease congestion in the Accident and Emergency (A&E) Department and reduce delays for patients awaiting admission.

The ward block forms part of a wider development programme to establish the medical city on 55.5 acres of land.

The proposed facility will include specialised clinical departments and diagnostic infrastructure to accommodate growing demand for advanced medical care.

Planned facilities include a 20-bed Intensive Care Unit (ICU), a 20-bed High Dependency Unit (HDU), a 600-bed Accident and Emergency facility, four operating theatres, 150 general ward beds, a central pharmacy and a diagnostic centre.

The development will also provide specialised clinics covering oncology, psychiatry, paediatrics, endocrinology, haematology, cardiology, dentistry, cardiothoracic services, renal care, gastroenterology, orthopaedics, forensic medicine and neurosurgery.

Research, training and support infrastructure

Beyond clinical services, the master plan incorporates six development zones to support healthcare delivery, medical training, research and staff welfare.

One zone will bring together the Kenya Medical Training College (KMTC), Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI), a blood bank, lecture amphitheatres and a resource centre.

The hospital also plans to construct multi-storey staff accommodation with 300 to 400 residential units and a separate Doctors’ Plaza.

Additional infrastructure will include a central warehouse, cold storage facilities, an aseptic pharmacy, a power substation and autoclave facilities. Plans also provide for general and executive farewell homes and an autopsy facility.

Environmental considerations feature in the design, with proposed investments in permeable grass-paver parking, sustainable urban drainage systems, flood detention facilities and landscaped healing gardens.

The development will comply with the Physical and Land Use Planning Act (Cap. 286).

Phased investment and hospital sustainability

Speaking during the unveiling, JOOTRH Acting Chief Executive Officer Dr Joshua Clinton Okise thanked Aprim Consultants for supporting the development of the master plan.

He urged newly appointed departmental heads to strengthen teamwork and take collective responsibility for implementing the hospital’s transformation programme.

The second phase will include development of Prime Care Hospital and Doctors’ Plaza, which are expected to generate additional revenue to support hospital operations and long-term financial sustainability.

The proposed expansion comes as regional referral hospitals face growing demand for specialised treatment, diagnostic services and critical care.

For JOOTRH, the planned investment will require sustained financing, coordinated infrastructure development and recruitment of specialised healthcare professionals to support the additional capacity.
